intro: Only the last week of November is left, so each deep dive is sized for about one week. Pick one, two or all three. Skipping is fine.

items.title: Superposition and sparse autoencoders in one week
items.why: Sparse autoencoders are the main tool for finding features inside language models. Knowing why they work, and where they fail, helps you read new interpretability papers critically.
items.objective: Explain superposition with a toy model, train a tiny sparse autoencoder yourself, and state one honest limit of the method.
prerequisites: linear algebra: projections and dot products

weeks.focus: Wed 25 to Fri 27 Nov: why neurons are polysemantic
tasks: Read Toy Models of Superposition: the overview, the first toy model and the phase-change sections
Do ARENA 1.3.2 part 0, Toy Models of Superposition, in Colab
Write three sentences: when does a model store more features than it has dimensions?

weeks.focus: Sat 28 to Mon 30 Nov: dictionary learning on a real model
tasks: Read Towards Monosemanticity: the summary, the problem setup and one feature case study such as base64 or Arabic script
Skim Cunningham et al. 2023 for how they test features causally on indirect object identification
Do ARENA 1.3.2 part 1, Intro to SAE interpretability, or train a small SAE with the SAELens guide
Read the GDM progress update steering section and note one result where SAE features did worse than a plain steering vector

primary_resource.creator: Callum McDougall (ARENA)
primary_resource.note: Self-contained Colab exercises. Part 3 covers training and evaluating SAEs if you want more.

resources.title: Progress Update #1 from the GDM Mech Interp Team
resources.creator: Nanda, Conmy, Smith, Rajamanoharan, Lieberum, Kramár, Varma
resources.note: Honest, tentative results on using SAE features for steering.

exercises: In the toy model, vary feature sparsity and watch when features start sharing dimensions
Pick one SAE feature and test it two ways: top activations and an ablation
items.deliverable: A one-page note: what superposition is, how an SAE untangles it, and one open problem.
items.definition_of_done: You can explain the L1 versus reconstruction trade-off and name one failure mode without notes.
items.final_synthesis: Write one research question that SAEs cannot yet answer well, and what evidence would settle it.
items.light_version: Read only the Towards Monosemanticity summary and one case study, then write the one-page note.
items.continuation: Possible later milestone: circuits built from SAE features, or SAEs for unlearning checks. Not scheduled automatically.

items.title: Concentration inequalities, derived by hand
items.why: Every generalization bound and many evaluation error bars rest on a few inequalities. Deriving them once makes them tools you can use, not facts you recall.
items.objective: Derive Markov, Chebyshev, Chernoff and Hoeffding from scratch, then use Hoeffding to bound the error of a finite hypothesis class.
prerequisites: the exponential function and Taylor series

weeks.focus: Wed 25 to Fri 27 Nov: from Markov to Chernoff
tasks: Read Vershynin, High-Dimensional Probability, Ch. 1 on basic inequalities and the start of Ch. 2
Prove Markov's inequality on paper. Then get Chebyshev from it in two lines
Derive the Chernoff method: apply Markov to exp(tX) and optimise over t

weeks.focus: Sat 28 to Mon 30 Nov: Hoeffding and a first learning bound
tasks: Prove Hoeffding's lemma for a bounded variable, then Hoeffding's inequality
Read Shalev-Shwartz and Ben-David, Ch. 2 to 4, and the concentration part of Appendix B
Derive the sample size needed for a finite hypothesis class to be agnostic PAC learnable

primary_resource.title: High-Dimensional Probability: An Introduction with Applications in Data Science
primary_resource.creator: Roman Vershynin
primary_resource.chapters: Ch. 1 and Ch. 2 up to Hoeffding
primary_resource.note: The author hosts a free draft on his university page. Link not verified this run.

resources.title: Understanding Machine Learning: From Theory to Algorithms
resources.creator: Shai Shalev-Shwartz and Shai Ben-David

resources.title: Understanding Machine Learning 2014: course lecture notes and videos
resources.creator: Shai Shalev-Shwartz
resources.note: Course that follows the book. Use the early PAC learning lectures.

exercises: Simulate coin flips in a notebook and plot the true tail probability against the Chebyshev and Hoeffding bounds
How many test examples do you need so a measured accuracy is within 1 point of the truth with 95 percent confidence?
items.deliverable: Handwritten derivations of all four inequalities, plus a short notebook comparing the bounds.
items.definition_of_done: You can rederive Hoeffding from a blank page and apply it to a benchmark error bar.
items.final_synthesis: Write a short note on what Hoeffding assumes, and which of those assumptions break for real benchmark data.
items.light_version: Only derive Markov, Chebyshev and Hoeffding, and do the test-set size exercise.
items.continuation: Possible later milestone: Rademacher complexity or martingale inequalities. Not scheduled automatically.

cross_domain.connection: The same inequality that proves learning is possible also tells you how big a test set must be before a benchmark gain means anything.

items.title: Draw Islamic geometric patterns with a compass and ruler
items.why: These patterns cover mosques and palaces from Spain to India. Drawing one by hand is calm, slow work, and it shows how a few circles hide a whole system of symmetry.
items.objective: Draw three patterns by hand from a single circle grid, and learn to spot their symmetries in real buildings.
prerequisites: a compass, a ruler, a pencil and paper
no art or maths background needed

weeks.focus: Wed 25 to Fri 27 Nov: look, then draw your first pattern
tasks: Read the Met essay Geometric Patterns in Islamic Art and look closely at its object images
Open the Smarthistory page on Eric Broug's explanation of how these designs come from a compass and ruler
Draw a simple eight-fold star pattern from one circle divided into eight, following Broug's step-by-step method

weeks.focus: Sat 28 to Mon 30 Nov: six-fold patterns and symmetry
tasks: Draw a six-fold pattern on a circle grid and repeat it to tile the page
Read the Heidelberg blog post on the Alhambra and the 17 wallpaper groups
Read Grünbaum's short article on whether all 17 groups really appear in the Alhambra
Find one building near you or online with a geometric pattern and name its rotation symmetry

primary_resource.title: Islamic Geometric Patterns
primary_resource.creator: Eric Broug
primary_resource.chapters: Technical tips, then the first eight-fold and six-fold patterns
primary_resource.note: Step-by-step drawing instructions. Library copies work well.

resources.title: The complex geometry of Islamic design
resources.creator: Eric Broug, via Smarthistory and TED-Ed

resources.title: The Palace of Alhambra and the Crystallographic Groups
resources.creator: Ana Chavez-Caliz, STRUCTURES blog, Heidelberg

resources.title: What Symmetry Groups Are Present in the Alhambra?
resources.creator: Branko Grünbaum, Notices of the AMS

exercises: Draw the same eight-fold star twice, once with only a compass and ruler and once freehand, and compare
Colour one tiled pattern so that the colouring has less symmetry than the lines
items.deliverable: Three hand-drawn patterns, one of them tiled across a full page.
items.definition_of_done: You can start from a blank page and draw an eight-fold star pattern without looking at the steps.
items.final_synthesis: Look at a pattern you did not draw and work out its starting circle grid.
items.light_version: Read the Met essay and draw just one eight-fold star.
items.continuation: Possible later milestone: ten-fold patterns, or coding a pattern generator. Not scheduled automatically.

cross_domain.connection: Craftsmen built these patterns with circles and lines. Mathematicians later classified the same repeats as wallpaper groups, and still argue about which ones the Alhambra contains.

plans.goal: Give a 30-second self-introduction out loud: name, where you are from, what you do, one hobby.

weeks.focus: Wed 25 and Thu 26: open and close politely
tasks: Learn はじめまして (hajimemashite, nice to meet you) and よろしくお願いします (yoroshiku onegaishimasu, please treat me kindly)
Say 〇〇です (〇〇 desu, I am 〇〇) out loud ten times with your name
Learn インドから来ました (Indo kara kimashita, I came from India)
Listen to one NHK Easy Japanese episode and shadow the greetings

weeks.focus: Sat 28 and Sun 29: work and a hobby
tasks: Learn 研究者です (kenkyūsha desu, I am a researcher) and 趣味は〇〇です (shumi wa 〇〇 desu, my hobby is 〇〇)
Role-play a first meeting with Claude, twice
Record your 30-second introduction on your phone and listen back once

plans.goal: Greet someone, ask how they are, and exchange names in Telugu.

tasks: Learn నమస్కారం (namaskāraṁ, hello) and say it out loud ten times
Learn బాగున్నారా? (bāgunnārā?, are you well?) and బాగున్నాను (bāgunnānu, I am well)
Learn మీ పేరు ఏమిటి? (mī pēru ēmiṭi?, what is your name?) and నా పేరు 〇〇 (nā pēru 〇〇, my name is 〇〇)
Watch the first lesson of Spoken Telugu Through English and repeat after the teacher
Role-play a greeting, how are you and names with Claude, then say it once without notes

notes: Manual late-month run. The earlier November package was removed because it used the old format, so this one covers only 25 to 30 Nov. Each deep dive is one week, split into two halves. Language plans use four short steps across the same days because the format needs four. The diffusion models idea stays in December. Vershynin's free draft link and the book site for Understanding Machine Learning could not be fetched, so those two books have no URL.
